S043.name: Restrictive_Intake
S043.description: Persistent restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to significantly low body weight.

subtypes.Eating Very Small Amounts: Eating only one or two bites a day or extremely small portions per meal.
subtypes.Skipping Meals: Intentionally skipping breakfast, lunch, or dinner.
subtypes.Exclusion of Specific Food Groups: Strictly avoiding specific food groups like carbohydrates or fats to prevent nutritional imbalance.
subtypes.Strict Calorie Restriction: Limiting daily caloric intake to an extremely low level.

S044.name: Low_Weight
S044.description: A body weight that is significantly below the minimum level of health for age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health.

subtypes.Continuous Weight Loss: A state where weight continues to decrease due to intentional restriction of intake.
subtypes.Insistence on Low Weight: Attempting to lose more weight or refusing to restore weight despite already being underweight.

S045.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
S045.description: Intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat, even though at a significantly low weight.

subtypes.Fear of Weight Gain: Extreme fear and loathing of gaining weight or becoming fat.
subtypes.Fear of Specific Foods: Fear that eating high-calorie foods will immediately lead to weight gain.
subtypes.Obsession with Weight Gain: Compulsively checking the scale and becoming extremely anxious about even the slightest increase.

S084.name: Low_Weight_Severity_Non_Recognition
S084.description: Persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight.

subtypes.Denial of Medical Risk: Not admitting or dismissing the health risks caused by being underweight.
subtypes.Disregard of Symptoms: Not taking physical symptoms caused by low weight (dizziness, hair loss, amenorrhea) seriously.
subtypes.Dismissal of Concerns: Exaggerating or rejecting the concerns of doctors or family as unnecessary.

symptom.disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by a persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and a disturbance in the way one’s body weight or shape is experienced. Patients often exhibit rigid dietary rules, overvaluation of thinness, and may deny the seriousness of their low weight despite medical compromise. Onset is most common in adolescence or young adulthood but can appear or recur later in life, often around stressful transitions or identity challenges, and the course can be chronic, relapsing, or episodic. It is distinguished from other eating disorders by the underweight status and primary focus on restriction rather than recurrent binge eating or overt compensatory behaviors like vomiting, although some individuals may also misuse exercise or other methods to influence weight.

patient.stressor: Tonya’s eating issues began to intensify when she started taking on larger, higher‑end residential projects and mentoring apprentices while studying for her certified lead‑painter credential. Long days on job sites, pressure to keep projects on tight timelines, and the physical demands of climbing ladders and hauling materials led her to focus increasingly on staying “lean and light” for work, which gradually shifted from a casual goal into a rigid preoccupation with controlling what she ate. As she began drafting business plans for her own sustainable finish company, the stress of proving herself in a male‑dominated trade and maintaining a certain image in front of eco‑conscious clients further reinforced her restrictive habits, even as friends noticed she was shrinking and skipping shared meals after weekend concerts or Habitat builds. She finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after nearly fainting on a ladder at a client’s home, which forced her to cancel jobs and scared both her apprentices and her parents, who insisted she get evaluated when they realized how much weight she had lost.
patient.chief_complaint: I’ve gotten so strict about what and how much I eat that I’m barely eating at all and it’s starting to interfere with my work on job sites.
